title: Tesla's Missing Autopilot Data Showed It Detected A Hazard Before Fatal Crash, Despite Claims It Was Missing

reading.body:
A Tesla vehicle with Autopilot engaged fatally crashed in 2024. Tesla told the victim's family that crash data from the vehicle was unavailable, but a security researcher recovered it through Tesla's bug bounty program, proving that all Tesla vehicles retain this information. The recovered data showed the vehicle had detected a hazard before the crash, contradicting Tesla's claim that the data did not exist.

This is a failure in data transparency and accountability in a safety-critical system. Tesla asserted as fact that evidence did not exist when it did, preventing the family and legal system from accessing information necessary to understand what the vehicle did during the crash. Detecting this would have required Tesla to verify its data retention claims before making statements to the family, and to conduct a thorough audit of what information was actually available rather than asserting its absence.

It is not established whether Tesla's initial claim about missing data resulted from negligence, a genuine misunderstanding of the system's architecture, or deliberate concealment. A jury found the company partially liable and a judge upheld a verdict of 243 million dollars in damages.

summary:
Tesla faced legal consequences after a 2024 fatal crash involving its self-driving vehicle. A jury determined the company was partially responsible for the incident, which killed Naibel Benavides Leon and injured Dillon Angulo. Tesla was ordered to pay 243 million dollars in damages and renamed its Autopilot and Full Self Driving features to emphasize that human supervision is required. The case concluded in February 2026 after a judge denied Tesla's appeal.

A critical piece of evidence emerged when a hacker, working through Tesla's Bug Bounty program, recovered crash data that Tesla claimed it did not possess. The company had told the grieving family that video recordings from the crash were unavailable, but the hacker proved that all Tesla vehicles retain this information. This recovered data proved instrumental in the jury's decision against Tesla. Meanwhile, Tesla crashes continue to rise, with driver-assist systems involved in 207 wrecks in May alone, the highest number recorded.
